h1: Belgian pale ale and English pale ale compared in the glass
title: Belgian vs English Pale Ale Compared | Craft Beer School
desc: Belgian and English pale ale side by side: malt, hops, yeast, strength, colour, carbonation and serving, with what to notice when you taste them.
teaser: Both are copper coloured ales around 5%. One tastes of biscuit and earthy hops, the other of pear and pepper. The yeast is why.
standfirst: Put a Belgian pale ale and an English pale ale next to each other and they look almost identical. Taste them and they are quite different beers. Here is what separates them and how to taste the difference yourself.
sections: Two pale ales from two traditions

English pale ale grew out of 19th century British brewing, when paler malts became affordable and brewers in Burton found their hard, sulphate rich water made crisp, bitter pale beers. Today the family includes ordinary bitter, best bitter and stronger pale ales, many served on cask in pubs. Our guide to English bitter covers that side in depth.

Belgian pale ale is a 20th century style from the Antwerp and Brabant area, brewed as an everyday beer that could compete with the pale lagers spreading across Europe. It is sometimes called spéciale belge. It shares a colour with its English cousin but comes from a brewing culture built around expressive yeast.

Using the BJCP guidelines as a reference:

  • Belgian pale ale: 4.8 to 5.5% ABV, 20 to 30 IBU, amber to copper in colour.
  • English best bitter: 3.8 to 4.6% ABV, 25 to 40 IBU, amber to light copper. Strong bitter, the closest English beer to a 5% pale ale, runs 4.6 to 6.2%.

So the English beer is usually a little weaker and noticeably more bitter. The Belgian beer is rounder, with less hop bite and more fruit from fermentation.

English pale ale is built on British pale ale malt, often with a little crystal malt. The result tastes of biscuit, bread crust and light caramel. Hops are English varieties like East Kent Goldings and Fuggle, which give earthy, floral, slightly herbal and marmalade notes. Bitterness is firm and lingers.

Belgian pale ale uses pilsner or pale malt with some Munich, Vienna or aromatic malt. It tastes of toasted bread and honey, a little nutty. Hops are restrained: Saaz, Styrian Goldings or similar, with a light spicy or floral touch rather than a bitter finish.

English ale yeast is fairly clean but gives some fruit, often described as apple, pear or stone fruit, plus a soft mineral feel. Some strains leave a hint of butterscotch from diacetyl, which a few traditional bitters carry at low levels.

Belgian yeast is far more expressive. Even in a moderate pale ale it adds orange, pear and a light peppery or clove like spice from phenols. That spice is the key tell. In an English pale ale, clove or pepper would be a fault. In a Belgian one, it is part of the style. Tasting them side by side is one of the best ways to learn what yeast alone contributes to a beer.

Cask English bitter is served lightly carbonated at cellar temperature, around 11 to 13 °C, through a hand pump into a pint glass. Bottled and kegged versions carry more fizz but are still modest. The low carbonation makes the malt and bitterness feel soft and full.

Belgian pale ale is served with medium to high carbonation and a firm head, often in a stemmed glass or goblet, at around 8 to 10 °C. The extra fizz lifts the yeast aromas and makes the beer feel lighter, even at higher strength.

In India, most bars serve everything at 2 to 4 °C. That flattens both beers. Let them sit a few minutes before you judge them.
How to taste them side by side

Pour both into the same shape of glass at the same temperature, roughly 10 °C. Smell first. Look for biscuit and earthy hop in the English beer, pear and pepper in the Belgian. Take a sip of each and pay attention to the finish: the English beer should leave a firm, dry bitterness, the Belgian a softer, slightly spicy one.

Then swap the order and taste again, because the first beer always changes how the second one tastes. Write three words for each. It sounds simple, but most people struggle at first to tell yeast fruit from hop fruit, or phenol spice from hop spice. Those distinctions are exactly what structured sensory training teaches. Our general guide to pale ale covers the American branch of the family too.
Food and finding them in India

English pale ale is good with fried food and anything roasted: fish fry, tandoori paneer, a mutton cutlet. Belgian pale ale suits lighter dishes with herbs and spice, such as a vegetable pulao or a Goan prawn dish.

Both are less common on Indian taps than wheat beers and IPAs. When a brewpub does pour one, ask whether it is a Belgian or English take. Brewers are usually happy to explain the yeast they chose. That conversation teaches you a lot.
faqs: What is the main difference between Belgian and English pale ale?
The yeast. Belgian yeast adds fruit and peppery spice, while English yeast is cleaner and lets malt and earthy hops lead.
English pale ale and bitter are usually more bitter. Belgian pale ale is rounder, with hops in a supporting role.
Is clove flavour a fault in English pale ale?
Yes. Clove or pepper from phenols is part of Belgian character but counts as a fault in an English pale ale.
